title: Who chairs the money committees, and whether lobbying follows the chair
question: Who chaired the Budget, Land Use, Rules and Government Audit committees each year, and do lobbyists’ contacts and their circles’ contributions concentrate on chairs more than on the other supervisors?
finding: From 2015 to 2026 the Board’s agendas and rosters give 67 supervisor-years in the chair of one of the four committees that hear money and land-use files. A chair was named in a typical 48 lobbying contacts a year, against 44 for the other supervisors sitting in the same years; the chairs’ typical figure was the higher one in 6 of 12 years. Comparing each supervisor with themselves, 8 had more contacts a year while chairing than while not and 7 had fewer (within what chance would produce). On the Land Use committee, the chair had more permit-and-planning contacts than the typical other supervisor in 10 of 12 years. Contributions from lobbyists, their firms’ staff and their clients’ staff came to a typical $200 in a chair-year and $2,000 in another supervisor’s year; 6 supervisors drew more of it while chairing and 9 less (within what chance would produce). The committees’ own roll calls on money files and lobbied measures (915 meetings of the four committees, 2015 to 2026) list 187 of the 217 member-years the agendas give, and add 4 member-years in which a supervisor sat at three or more meetings of a committee without being on an agenda on disk. In 573 cases a money file sent on by a committee named an organization already in the donor circle of a supervisor then on the Board; that supervisor sat on the committee in 129 of them (22.5%), where the same supervisors’ share of committee seats on files of the same kind in those years would give about 141 (24.6%): within what chance would produce. Member by member, 9 sat more often than their seat share predicts by more than half a file and 13 less often.
how: Committee membership is read from the “Board Committees” box printed on the Board’s agendas (the first meeting of each year and of each July, 2015 to 2026), which names the chair first and the vice-chair second; the legacy office records to 2018; and the 2026 committee roster and President’s memos. Budget and Finance and Budget and Appropriations are counted as one family, and joint or select committees are left out. A supervisor has a chair-year when any of those sources names them chair of one of the four families in that calendar year. Contacts are registered lobbyists’ reported contacts naming that supervisor in that year. “Circle giving” is itemised money to the supervisor’s candidate committees in that year from registered lobbyists, from donors who wrote a lobbying firm or a lobbying client as employer, and from those firms and clients in their own name. Two comparisons are made: chairs against the other supervisors sitting in the same year, and each supervisor’s chair-years against their own other years on the Board (a sign test: how many go up, how many down, and what a coin would give). The roll-call columns come from the vote grids of the committees themselves (roll calls on money files and lobbied measures, 2015 to 2026, through the shared roll-call reader): a member “sat” at a meeting when a grid of that committee on that day lists the member, whatever vote is printed. They check the agendas and add members the two yearly snapshots miss. For the last comparison, each money file that a committee recommended or referred to the Board and that names an outside organization (grants the City accepts left out) is paired with every supervisor then on the Board who already had that organization in their donor circle; the count of those supervisors who sat on the committee is set against what their share of committee seats would give (of all money files naming an outside organization that any committee sent on in the same calendar year, the share sent on by a committee listing that supervisor), by drawing each case ten thousand times at that share.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt, and contacting the chair of the committee that hears a client’s file is ordinary, registered lobbying. Chairs are also often senior members with more legislation of their own, which draws contacts for reasons that have nothing to do with the gavel. Contributions follow the election calendar far more than committee seats, so the giving comparison is weak; contact reports name aides as often as supervisors, and those contacts are not counted here. The agendas are two snapshots a year, so a chair who served a few months between them is missed. Files go to a committee by subject, not by counterparty: the Budget and Finance Committee hears nearly every contract and grant, so its members sit on most files whoever is named in them, and the staff of organizations in a field give to the supervisors who work on that field. Several supervisors can be paired with one file, so the cases are not independent and the test overstates certainty. A committee grid lists a substitute member like a regular one. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
